key_insight: The paper shows that long-studied nuclear symmetries, especially SU(3) and SU(4), can be turned into interpretable neural-network features that help explain nuclear masses across the chart. Instead of chasing only prediction accuracy, the models aim to reveal whether fundamental symmetry structure still governs binding energy globally.
problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of modeling nuclear masses in a way that is both physically meaningful and interpretable. Traditional high-accuracy methods can work well but often obscure the underlying physics, while ab initio symmetry ideas have mostly been tested in lighter nuclei rather than across the full nuclear landscape.
method: Derive input features from SU(3) and SU(4) Casimir operators, which encode symmetry information from nuclear structure.
Build interpretable neural-network mass models, including a Feature-Informed NN (FINN) for point predictions and related Gaussian-informed variants.
Use these symmetry-aware models to test whether ab initio symmetries provide useful global guidance for nuclear binding, prioritizing insight over pure predictive performance.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this is a strong example of physics-informed and interpretable learning: models are designed around domain theory rather than opaque end-to-end fitting. It highlights how embedding known structure into neural networks can improve scientific understanding, not just prediction quality.

paper_title: Bridging Ab Initio Symmetries and Global Nuclear Masses with Interpretable Neural Networks
paper_authors: Phong Dang, Evander Espinoza, Xiaoliang Wan, Michela Negro, Jerry P. Draayer
